questions: When you want to learn something new, do you prefer to be taught or to figure it out yourself?
What's the most recent thing you've tried to learn, big or small?
Why do you think some people pick up new skills so much faster than others?
Were you a different kind of learner at school than you are now?
Is there something you keep meaning to learn but never actually start?
What does a typical weekday evening look like for you?
Do you have anything you do most evenings, almost without thinking?
Some people say they can't relax without a screen on. Is that true for you?
Did your evenings look different five or ten years ago?
Do you think you'll spend your evenings differently as you get older?

part2.title: Describe something useful you learned unexpectedly, outside school or work.
bullets: what you learned and roughly when this happened
how you came to learn it
who or what helped you learn it
why you weren't expecting to learn it
part2.explain: and explain why this has turned out to be useful, and whether you'd have learned it as well in a classroom.
followups: Have you passed this on to anyone else?
Do you use it more or less than when you first learned it?
Was there a moment you realised it had actually become useful?

part3.q: Think about the most useful things people know. How many of them were learned by accident rather than by plan?
followups: Why might accidental learning stick so well?
Can you plan for the accidents — put yourself in their way?

part3.q: What can someone learn from fixing a leaking tap or cooking for ten people that a course could never teach them?
followups: Is it the knowledge that's different, or the way it's acquired?
Does the risk of failing matter to the learning?

part3.q: Almost any skill can now be learned free from internet videos. Has that genuinely changed who gets to learn, or just who gets to watch?
followups: What separates the people who finish from the people who browse?
What's still missing from learning this way?

part3.q: If a self-taught programmer and a computer science graduate apply for the same job, who should get it, and what should decide?
followups: Why do employers still lean on certificates?
Is there a fair way to prove a skill you taught yourself?

part3.q: Some people say curiosity fades with age; others say adults just stop being given permission to be beginners. Which is closer to the truth?
followups: Why is it socially harder to be a beginner at fifty than at fifteen?
What would make it easier?

part3.q: Why do so many adults say they learned more in their first year of work than in years of formal study?
followups: Is that a criticism of education, or just a different kind of learning?
Could schools realistically recreate that?

part3.q: Schools mostly reward learning that can be tested. What happens to the kinds of learning that can't be?
followups: Can you give an example of something valuable but untestable?
Who decides what counts as learning?

part3.q: Should formal education try to absorb informal learning — grading hobbies, certifying life skills — or would that destroy what makes it work?
followups: What is it about measurement that changes an activity?
Is there a middle path?

part3.q: In a world where knowledge goes out of date quickly, is knowing how to learn now worth more than any particular thing you know?
followups: Can 'learning how to learn' actually be taught, or only practised?
Does anything stay permanently worth knowing?

part3.q: Imagine formal education did adapt fully to how people actually learn. What would it have to give up?
followups: Who would resist that change most?
Would anything important be lost along the way?

fc: Tells the Part 2 story as a discovery — the accident, the learning, the payoff — in one connected arc rather than a list of facts about a skill.
Uses time-shifting markers fluently ("at the time I had no idea", "it was only months later that", "looking back") because this card lives in two time frames: learning it, and realising it mattered.
Thinks aloud convincingly on the harder Part 3 questions: "That's a distinction I hadn't considered — my instinct says permission, and here's why…" reads as fluency, not hesitation.
Extends answers without prompting — for the credentials question, weighs both candidates before the examiner reaches for a follow-up.
Keeps register steady when the topic jumps from evenings on the sofa to the purpose of education — no sudden lurch into memorised formal English.
lr: Learning vocabulary with real range: pick up, trial and error, muscle memory, rule of thumb, learning curve, get the hang of, self-taught, hands-on.
Separates near-synonyms cleanly: study vs learn vs master; qualification vs skill vs experience — and deploys the right one under pressure.
Evening and leisure language that sounds lived-in: wind down, switch off, potter about, lose track of time — not textbook 'leisure activities'.
Abstract Part 3 lexis handled naturally: credential, competence, incentive, intrinsic motivation, obsolete, lifelong learning — without sounding like an education journal.
Paraphrases smoothly when a term is missing: "the certificate — the piece of paper that proves it" keeps the answer moving and shows resourcefulness.
gra: Past habitual forms for the backstory: "I used to watch my uncle do it", "I'd never have bothered if the shop hadn't been shut."
Third conditional and mixed conditionals earn their keep on this card: "If I'd learned it in a classroom, I doubt it would have stayed with me."
Comparative clauses that carry the Part 3 argument: "the more measurable a skill is, the more schools value it — and the reverse worries me."
Modality graded precisely across the credentials question: "must prove", "ought to count", "might reasonably prefer" — not one modal stretched over everything.
Gerund and infinitive patterns accurate under speed: "worth knowing", "stopped bothering to", "permission to be a beginner", "no way of proving".
pron: Contrastive stress does the arguing: "I didn't MEAN to learn it — that's exactly WHY it stuck."
The word 'learn' and its family recur constantly in this test — vowel length in 'learn/learnt/learner' stays clear and doesn't collapse into 'lun'.
Chunking matches the thought: "knowing how to learn | is worth more | than anything you happen to know" delivered in meaningful groups, not word by word.
Intonation lifts genuine curiosity in the reflective questions — a flat delivery makes 'that's an interesting question' sound like its opposite.
Multi-syllable topic words — curiosity, certificate, obsolete, autodidact if you dare — stressed on the right syllable or swapped for a safer word.

band9.part1: Answer in two to four sentences: commit, then ground it in something real. For "When you want to learn something new, do you prefer to be taught or to figure it out yourself?" a Band 9 answer sounds like this: "Figure it out myself, at least at first — I learned basic video editing entirely by ruining my cousin's wedding montage and starting over twice. I only look for a teacher once I know exactly what I can't do." It answers the actual either/or, admits something imperfect, and gives one concrete detail — no prepared speech about the importance of education.
part2: Opening / context — name the thing you learned in the first sentence, plainly: 'how to read a train timetable in another language', 'how to calm someone having a panic attack'. Mystery openings waste seconds.
The accident — describe the situation that forced or invited the learning: the broken thing, the emergency, the boredom, the favour you couldn't refuse. This bullet is where 'unexpectedly' lives.
The learning itself — how it actually went: who showed you, what you got wrong first, the moment it clicked. One honest failure makes the whole story credible.
Who or what helped — a named person, a video channel, an old manual. Give them one line of character; it turns a report into a story.
The payoff — a specific occasion since when this knowledge earned its keep. 'Useful' is the card's key word: prove it with an incident, not an adjective.
Concluding sentence — answer the classroom question head-on: would a course have taught you this as well? Say why or why not in one line, and stop.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: If a self-taught programmer and a computer science graduate apply for the same job, who should get it, and what should decide?
framework: Answer: take a clear position — e.g. whoever performs better on work that resembles the actual job; the route they took to competence should be close to irrelevant.

Explain: give the mechanism — a degree is a proxy signal that made sense when skills were hard to verify directly; once you can test the skill itself, paying extra attention to the proxy is a habit, not a reason.
Example: one concrete illustration — plenty of software firms now hire through practical assignments and portfolio review, and some of their strongest engineers never finished a formal program.

Alternative view: concede genuinely — the graduate's degree can certify breadth the self-taught coder may lack: theory, fundamentals, the unglamorous parts nobody teaches themselves voluntarily; for some roles that depth is the job.

Evaluate: land the judgement — so the fair decider is a task, not a title: test what the work needs, let the credential break ties at most — and expect hiring to keep drifting this way as skills get easier to verify directly.

mistakes.title: Choosing a school subject for the cue card
mistakes.detail: The card says outside school or work — twice, effectively. Describing how you unexpectedly enjoyed chemistry class contradicts the prompt in the first sentence, and examiners notice immediately.

mistakes.title: Dropping the 'unexpectedly'
mistakes.detail: The fourth bullet — why you weren't expecting to learn it — is the whole personality of this card. A story about deliberately signing up for a cooking course answers a different, easier card, and loses the marks the surprise would have earned.

mistakes.title: Naming the skill but never the learning
mistakes.detail: Candidates spend the two minutes explaining what the skill is — how baking works, what first aid involves — and never describe learning it: the fumbling, the helper, the moment it clicked. The card asks for the second story, not a tutorial.

mistakes.title: Claiming usefulness without evidence
mistakes.detail: "It's very useful in my daily life" is an assertion. One specific occasion when the skill rescued you — a real evening, a real problem — is worth more than three sentences of general praise.

mistakes.title: One-line evening answers
mistakes.detail: "What does a typical evening look like?" answered with "I watch TV and sleep." starves the examiner. Add when, what, and one honest detail — the show you're embarrassed to enjoy does more for your score than a dignified lie.

mistakes.title: The rehearsed 'internet is a double-edged sword' speech
mistakes.detail: The self-teaching question asks who actually benefits, not for a balanced essay on technology. Memorised advantage-disadvantage frames surface instantly and answer nothing.

mistakes.title: Sitting on the fence about credentials
mistakes.detail: "Both candidates have merits" with no follow-through is a Band 6 pattern. Pick the programmer or the graduate — or name the deciding test — and defend the choice. Commitment plus reasoning is what the question is fishing for.

mistakes.title: Only personal examples in Part 3
mistakes.detail: "I taught myself guitar, so self-teaching works" is one data point. Band 8–9 answers generalise — 'most people who start free courses', 'employers in practical fields' — and use the personal case as seasoning, not the meal.

mistakes.title: Treating the curiosity question as flattery bait
mistakes.detail: "Old people can learn too, my grandmother uses WhatsApp" dodges the actual fork: does curiosity fade, or is permission withdrawn? The question hands you two theories — engage with both, then choose.

mistakes.title: Overusing 'nowadays' as an engine
mistakes.detail: This topic tempts candidates into starting every Part 3 answer with 'Nowadays, with the development of technology…'. It's filler, it's flagged as memorised, and the answer hasn't started yet. Start with your position instead.
